asDecan.p: Your Sun sits in the first ten degrees of Aquarius, which the Golden Dawn handed to Venus. Venus has no special standing in Aquarius. It's a visitor there, and it picks up the manners of the sign's ruler, Saturn in the old system and Uranus in the modern one. So you get Aquarius at its freshest, fixed air that makes up its mind and keeps it, with Venus adding a real liking for people and a strong sense of what's fair. The catch is that Venus wants closeness and Aquarius wants to be right, and the Five of Swords is what happens when those two end up in the same argument. Mercury runs the next ten degrees and gets the Six, which is about moving on. The Moon takes the last slice and the Seven. The Star is your Sun card, the wide view of Aquarius, and this is the finer grain inside it. Look at the man in the picture, picking up swords while two people walk off.

You like people, lots of them, and you're usually the one who knows everyone at the party a little. But let a group chat turn into a debate about something you care about, whether the landlord's allowed to do that or whether a film was actually any good, and you'll stay up until one sending careful, reasonable paragraphs. At a family lunch you're the one who corrects your uncle's facts, politely, and then can't work out why the mood went flat. When a friend cancels on you twice you don't say you're hurt. You say it's fine, and you mean it in principle. You'd rather be fair than be close, and most of the time you don't notice you've made that choice. A Sunday with nothing planned tends to fill up with friends, and you can still feel a bit on your own in the middle of them.

What people underestimate is how well you can separate a person from their opinion. Venus here takes on some of Saturn's backbone, so you can tell a friend her business plan has a hole in it and still be at her birthday the following week, with neither of you holding it against the other. In a meeting where everyone's nodding along to a bad idea because the boss likes it, you're often the one who says, quite calmly, that the numbers don't add up, and you sit through the awkward silence without flinching. You don't hold grudges about ideas either. Someone can shout you down in a debate and you'll buy them a drink afterwards. I see this a lot in early Aquarius Suns, and it makes you very good company for anyone who actually wants an honest opinion.

The less obvious one is what you do with other people's feelings. Your partner comes home upset about a colleague and within two minutes you're explaining the colleague's side, because it's only fair, and your partner goes quiet and goes off to have a shower. You were right about the colleague, which is a bit of a problem. There's another habit too. When an argument turns personal, you often stop arguing altogether and just leave, sometimes the room and sometimes the friendship, and you tell yourself it was the grown-up thing to do. The friend who fell out with you over a wedding seating plan three years ago probably still doesn't know why you went cold. You're generous with strangers and with causes, and a bit stingier with the four or five people who actually need you.

When something goes badly, a redundancy or a break-up or a friend saying something cruel, your first move is to work out who was in the right. You'll lay it out for anyone who asks, calmly and in order, and people may think you're coping brilliantly. A week later you're usually still arguing it, only now it's in your head at two in the morning and you're drafting a message you'll never send. You get cooler with everyone, even people who had nothing to do with it, and they feel the draught without knowing where it's coming from. What actually helps is letting one person be on your side without asking them to be fair. Tell them it hurt, let them say the other person was awful, and don't correct them.

You tend to fall for people by arguing with them. The first proper conversation that runs past midnight, where they disagree with you and don't back down, does more for you than flowers ever could. Venus in a Saturn-ruled sign likes a bit of resistance. The part people miss is that you also need to lose sometimes, to someone you respect, and a partner who always gives in to keep the peace slowly bores you, even if you'd never say so. Where it goes wrong is the small fights, whose turn it was to ring the plumber, who forgot to book the anniversary dinner, which you can win on the facts every single time. Try letting your partner have the last word on something minor and see what it does to the next few days.

Work that runs on a principle suits you. Advocacy, policy, community organising, user research, editing, law, running a volunteer group, any job where you get to argue for the people who aren't in the room. You also have a good eye, which is the Venus in you, so design with a social point to it tends to pull you in. The pattern to watch is the internal fight. There's a restructure or a new process and you can see exactly why it's wrong, so you write the email, and you're right, and it goes through your way. Then you notice nobody's asked you to lunch for a month. Before a big meeting it's worth deciding which two issues you'll go to the wall over, and letting the rest slide, even the ones you'd win.

At twenty this decan is often at its most combative. You've got strong views on nearly everything, you'll happily argue with a lecturer or a manager in front of everyone, and you lose a few friends to it without much regret. By the mid-thirties most people with the Sun here have won at least one fight that cost them more than they expected, a sibling they stopped speaking to or a workplace they had to leave, and they get choosier. The views are still there. They just stop needing everyone to agree. The fifties tend to bring a warmer version of the same person, still the one who says the awkward thing at the committee meeting, only with more humour, and the people who've stuck around are usually the ones who were always willing to argue back.

Next time you feel the urge to correct someone in a group, a date, a statistic, a bit of history they've got slightly wrong, let it go and see if anything bad happens. Keep a quiet tally in the notes on your phone for a fortnight. Mostly nothing does. When it's a friend or a partner who's upset, ask one question before you offer any view at all, something like 'what did you want them to do?', and then just listen to the answer.
